Madhav waited by the colony gate at five, the way he had every evening since Class 2, with the carrom striker in his pocket.

Farida came out at ten past, but she was with two girls from her dance class, and she only waved. "Can't today, Madhav! Practice!"

It was the fourth time that week.

He went up the stairs slowly. At dinner he pushed his dal around and asked his mother, "Did I do something to Farida?"

"Did you fight?"

"No." That was the strange part. There had been no fight. She still smiled at him in the lift. She just wasn't there anymore.

That night he lay awake going through every day of the last month, looking for the thing he had done wrong, and not finding it.

qa.a: The carrom striker.

qa.q: Why does Madhav lie awake going through the last month?
qa.a: He feels a dull hurt and confusion, wondering what he did wrong, because there was no fight to explain why Farida drifted away.

qa.q: What could Madhav's mother say that might help him?
qa.a: She could explain that friends sometimes get busy with new things like dance class, and that it may not be about anything he did; she could also help him ask Farida gently.

qa.q: How might Farida see these evenings?
qa.a: She is probably just busy and excited about dance practice and her new friends, and may not realise how much Madhav is missing her.

grounding: Madhav feels a dull ache and wonders what he did when Farida drifts toward her dance friends, although the real cause is new company and a busier schedule.

When Lavanya started playing badminton with the girls from 6B, I stopped talking to her. I thought that was fair, because she had stopped talking to me first.

Amma noticed. She didn't lecture me. She just asked, "Do you miss her?"

I said no. Then I cried.

The next morning Amma walked with me to the school gate and said, "Just say hello. That's all. You don't have to fix anything."

So I did. Lavanya looked surprised, then she said hello back and smiled.

On Saturday Amma helped me invite her to our building's treasure hunt. She came. We had fun, even if it wasn't like before.

Amma said some friends are for one season and some for many, and a season ending doesn't make the good part fake. I think about that when I see Lavanya now.

— Shreya

Rafiq has been moping since Disha started spending lunch with the robotics kids. He said, "She was never really my friend," and slammed his door.

I didn't argue. At bedtime I asked what he missed most. "Building forts with her," he said.

I told him that some friends are close in one season and further away in another, and that the forts they built were real. He said, "So it wasn't fake?" I said, "No. It was real."

There had been no fight. No moment he could point to. They had lived in the same corridor for three years at university; Oskar had driven him to the hospital the night he broke his wrist.

Emil put the phone in his pocket and looked out at the grey harbour. He felt something close to grief, and then felt a bit silly for it. Nobody had died. Nobody had even left. It had just... faded.

The college library in Pune was almost empty during the holidays. Sudha had come to return a book and found herself sitting at the table by the window, the one where she and Omkar had spent all of second year.

Their initials were still scratched faintly under the edge. S + O, study partners, not the other thing, they used to joke.

She tried to remember the last time they had actually talked. Not a "congrats!!" under a post, but talked. It must have been before his internship, before her exams. Eight months, maybe nine.

Nothing had happened. They hadn't fought. It was just that each week had been busy, and then it had been a year.

Sudha sat there longer than she meant to. When the librarian began switching off the lights, her eyes were wet, and she didn't quite know how to explain why.

Sabina,

I'm not sure I'll send this.

I was clearing my phone last night and found our old voice notes from first year, the ones where we narrated each other's bad days like cricket commentary. I laughed out loud, alone in my room, and then I didn't feel like laughing.

I tried to remember our last real conversation. I think it was when your grandmother was unwell, in February. Since then, it's been hearts on photos and "we should catch up!!" that neither of us followed through.

Nothing went wrong. I keep looking for the moment, and there isn't one. That's the part that's hard to explain to anyone. You can't say "I lost a friend" when nobody left.

But it feels like I did.

Nitin

Dear Tejas,

I've been meaning to write this for weeks and kept waiting for the right moment. There isn't one, so here it is.

Yesterday I walked past the chai stall near our old college gate, and the man still had that chipped blue kettle. I thought of all our Sunday evenings there, arguing about films and planning lives we didn't end up living.

Noor

You asked how I handle old friendships after college. I'm Rekha, and I'll tell you about Sarita and me.

For about a year, we barely talked. Nothing happened. She moved to Kochi, I started work. I kept waiting for her to call, and I think she was waiting for me.

Then one night I found a photo of us at the Durga Puja pandal, faces covered in sindoor, laughing like idiots. I didn't write "hey, long time". I wrote, "I was thinking of that Puja night. Can we talk on Sunday?"

She called on Sunday. We talked for three hours.

But I'll be honest: I also had a friend from hostel, Lata, and when I thought about messaging her, I felt nothing. So I didn't. I just felt thankful for what we had.

Some you chase, some you let go with thanks. Both are allowed.

qa.a: Rekha felt no pull to reach out to Lata, only grateful and at peace about what they had, so chose to let that friendship go.

My roommate Lavanya had been moody all week, and on Thursday night I found out why.

She was sitting on her bed with her phone, typing and deleting. "It's Gautam," she said. "From school. We used to study together every evening. We haven't talked properly since he moved to Delhi."

She showed me her drafts: "Hi! Long time!" deleted. "How are you??" deleted.

Then she typed, slowly, "I was thinking of those evenings on your terrace doing maths. Can we talk on Saturday?" and sent it before she could delete it.

She put the phone face down and let out a long breath.

Gautam replied twenty minutes later: "YES. I miss that terrace." She laughed out loud.

I don't know what they talked about on Saturday. I only know she hummed all Sunday.

— Deepti

Hafsa, beta, you asked me once who my first real friend was. It was Kamla, in Jabalpur, when I was fifteen and she was fourteen.
